hypotheses.statement: Cerebrolysin as an add-on therapy for moderate-severe acute ischemic stroke is cost-effective versus standard care at a willingness-to-pay threshold of 50,000 EUR per QALY over a 90-day horizon.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: Probabilistic sensitivity analysis results indicate an 80% chance probability of cost-effectiveness of Cerebrolysin as an add-on therapy for acute ischemic stroke, considering a willingness-to-pay threshold of 50,000 EUR in a 90-day timeframe after stroke.

hypotheses.statement: The Cerebrolysin and placebo arms of the retained 193-patient subsample are comparable at baseline.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: No major differences were found, allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups.

tests.provenance_quote: We compared baseline characteristics (demographics, stroke severity, social and medical history) of the 193 patients for whom we calculated QALYs. No major differences were found, allowing for a relevant comparison of health outcomes between the Cerebrolysin and placebo groups.
The lowest ICER values were determined based on the ordinal valuation (18,788 EUR/QALY), while the highest were concluded for the Bayesian posterior valuation method (26,981 EUR/QALY).

Based on the CARS trial patient pathway, the Cerebrolysin add-on treatment was cost-effective in roughly 80% of cases for an ICER threshold set at 50,000 EUR (Figure 2 and Figure 3), considering only the 90-day timeframe of the CARS-study.

findings.location: Table 1, Standard Treatment column (Median row against Mean, Standard deviation and Sample size rows)

consequence.explanation: The reported placebo median (1767 EUR) exceeds the reported Cerebrolysin median (1466 EUR), reversing the direction of the paper's central cost comparison -- that Cerebrolysin costs 408 EUR more per patient than standard care -- which is the numerator of every ICER reported.

findings.notes: This is the strongest finding in the paper. A median of 1767 requires at least half the sample to sit at or above 1767, i.e. at or above 7.10 standard deviations above the reported mean of 1050. Cantelli's inequality caps the achievable share at 0.0195, so no distribution whatsoever -- not merely no normal one -- can carry mean 1050, SD 101 and median 1767 simultaneously; the tool reports distribution_free_violation = true, so the verdict does NOT rest on a normality assumption about skewed cost data. Inputs were re-read from the get_table grid before flagging. The remaining Table 1 statistics are mutually coherent (see cerebrolysin_median_consistent, ci_consistency_both_arms), which isolates this single cell: SD 101 with n = 93 reproduces the printed 95% bounds almost exactly, so the mean, SD and interval agree and only the median dissents. The most economical explanation is a transcription error (e.g. 1067 mis-set as 1767), but as printed the row is not internally satisfiable. I have recorded the tool's own severity of highly_suspicious rather than escalating to impossible: the Cantelli contradiction is exact arithmetic, and the editorial stage may reasonably treat it as such. The supplementary Cost worksheet contains the per-patient costs that would settle this immediately.

findings.location: Supplementary dataverse workbook, QALY worksheet, rows 119 and 120 (patient_ID P-2-29 and P-2-32)

consequence.explanation: If duplicated records are genuine rather than tied health states, the placebo-arm QALY mean of 0.156-0.171 that forms every ICER denominator rests on a sample containing repeated observations.

findings.notes: Recorded at suspicious although the tool returned highly_suspicious, and the reason is specific. The aggregate count is inflated by two classes of legitimate repetition that rulebook rule 11 requires me to discount first: (a) design constants -- the value 207.9 recurs 93 times in a single contiguous run in Cost column K, and 93 is exactly the placebo arm size, so this is an arm-level constant I should have passed in exclude_columns; and (b) finite-lookup ties -- SF-6D utilities come from a discrete converter, so single values recur heavily by construction (0.6166 appears 27 times in one column, 0.6228 and 0.7476 four times each). What those guards do NOT explain is the row-pair signal, which I verified directly against the raw grid rather than trusting the aggregate: patients P-2-29 and P-2-32, two distinct placebo IDs, carry identical values in all nine numeric columns -- six independent utility lookups at two separate visits plus three derived QALYs agreeing to 17 significant figures. That is possible innocently only if both patients returned the same SF-6D health state at BOTH visit 2 and visit 7. 75 such pairs were flagged and row-pair coverage is PARTIAL, so 75 is a floor, not a count. Adjudicating this needs the underlying SF-36 item responses, which are not in the workbook. Only one pair was individually verified; the other 74 are asserted by the tool and unexamined.

findings.quote: By doing so, we can assert that there are no potential variations in preferences and risk attitudes which may impact the overall cost-effectiveness analysis.

inputs.claim: no potential variations in preferences and risk attitudes

consequence.explanation: The sentence claims the choice of valuation model does not matter, when the paper's own three ICERs span roughly 8,200 EUR/QALY and the abstract presents that spread as its headline range.

findings.notes: Recorded as a textual flag in a load-bearing sentence (rulebook section 7), not as an arithmetic finding. Running three valuation models cannot establish that no variation in preferences exists; at most it shows the direction of the conclusion is stable. The paper's own results contradict the sentence directly, since the three models produce the range the abstract reports as 18.8 to 29.9 thousand EUR. The preceding sentence in the same paragraph states the opposite intent ('can offer valuable insights into the robustness and sensitivity of the derived utility scores'), which suggests a drafting inversion rather than a substantive claim. Two smaller errors sit nearby and are noted only because they co-occur: 'we argue the threshold itself if not relevant' (Discussion, for 'is not relevant'), and the incident-stroke count written as 'n = 37.225' with a decimal point used as a thousands separator in an otherwise English-convention paper.

unchecked.location: Table 2, Deterministic ICER column (18,788 / 20,618 / 26,981 EUR per QALY)
unchecked.reason: No validated tool in this toolkit computes or verifies an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Reproducing these three values from the stated incremental cost of 408 EUR and the Table 2 QALY increments would require hand division, which I have not performed. This is the paper's primary outcome and it is therefore the largest hole in this review. A reader should specifically check two things: whether 408 EUR divided by each printed QALY increment reproduces the printed ICER, and whether the ordering is internally coherent -- the ordinal row has a SMALLER Cerebrolysin-minus-placebo QALY increment than the standard gamble row (0.182 vs 0.168, against 0.186 vs 0.171) yet is reported with the LOWER ICER (18,788 vs 20,618), which cannot hold if all three ICERs share the same 408 EUR numerator.

unchecked.location: Results paragraph 2 / Methods 2.2 - currency conversion of 7214 RON to 1458 EUR at 1 EUR = 4.95 RON
unchecked.reason: Verifying a currency conversion requires hand division and no validated tool covers it. Flagged for a reader because the placebo figure (5197 RON to 1050 EUR) and the Cerebrolysin figure appear to round in different directions at the same stated rate.

unchecked.location: Discussion, paragraph 6 - budget impact 'roughly 8.5 million EUR per year'
unchecked.reason: This is a product of a national incident count, two assumed proportions (80% ischemic, two-thirds moderate-severe) and a unit cost. No validated tool multiplies counts by unit costs, and performing the arithmetic by hand is outside the tool discipline for this stage.

Anything read off the plotted marks would be figure_pixels provenance and barred from the exact-arithmetic checks, so the probabilistic sensitivity analysis -- which supports the abstract's headline claim -- is essentially unverifiable from the published article.
